instruction: Who is the person who keeps coming to check my arm where the tube is?
response: That's your nurse! You have a nurse who is specially assigned to take care of you. Their job is to check on you regularly — even at nighttime — to make sure you're comfortable and that everything is working the way it should. They also help coordinate your appointments and make sure your family knows what's going on. If the tube in your arm is ever bugging you, you can tell your nurse and they'll help.

instruction: Why did that lady ask me to draw a picture about how I'm feeling?
response: She's probably the art therapist! The art therapy program at Children's Hospital gives kids a chance to share their thoughts and feelings through creative stuff like drawing, painting, or crafting. You don't have to be good at art — it's not about making something perfect. It's just a fun way to express what's going on inside when it's hard to find the right words. You can draw whatever you want!

instruction: There's a clown walking around. Is this a real hospital?
response: Yes, it's a real hospital! That clown is named Ollie, and Ollie is a therapeutic clown. That's a special person trained to bring play, laughter, and fun to kids in the hospital. Ollie's job is to help make your time here feel a little more normal and a lot more cheerful. Hospitals can feel serious, but having someone like Ollie around reminds everyone that fun and silliness are still allowed!

instruction: Someone came in and said they're a resident. Are they living here?
response: Ha, no — they don't actually live at the hospital! A resident is a doctor who has already finished medical school and is now getting extra training in a special area, like taking care of kids. They work with your main doctor to help figure out the best plan for you. Think of them like a doctor who's still learning even more so they can be the best they can be.

instruction: What does the person with the guitar do?
response: That's the music therapist! They use music to help kids feel better while they're in the hospital. Music therapy can help with things like pain and just feeling more relaxed. The cool part is you don't need to know how to play any instrument or sing well to join in — anyone can take part. You might get to play instruments, sing, or just listen. It's one of the neat things Children's Hospital offers.

instruction: A lady said she's a child life specialist. What does that mean?
response: A Child Life Specialist is someone whose whole job is to help kids and their families handle being in the hospital. They're trained to explain what's going to happen before a procedure so it's not as scary, help you find ways to cope with things that hurt or feel weird, and help you express your feelings through play. They're kind of like your personal guide to making the hospital less overwhelming. If you're nervous about anything, they're a great person to talk to!

instruction: Someone new came in this morning and said they're my nurse now. What happened to my other nurse?
response: Nothing happened to your other nurse — they're totally fine! Nurses work in shifts, so after a certain number of hours, a new nurse takes over. When that happens, the two nurses do something called a bedside shift change report, where they talk about how you're doing and what the plan is. Your parent or guardian can listen in and ask questions too. Your new nurse will introduce themselves, and they'll know all about your care because the other nurse told them everything.

instruction: What's a dietitian? Somebody called a dietitian came to talk to my mom.
response: A dietitian is a person who knows a whole lot about food and what your body needs to stay healthy, especially when you're sick or recovering. They might have been talking to your mom about what kinds of food are best for you right now, or about any special diet you might need. At Children's Hospital, the food you get is actually chosen based on what your doctor and dietitian think will help you the most. If you have favourite foods or things you can't eat, your family can let them know!

instruction: A dog came to visit today! Whose dog is that?
response: That's a therapy dog! Children's Hospital has a special program with St. John Ambulance where trained therapy dogs come to visit kids. The dogs are super friendly and calm, and spending time with them can help you feel happier and more relaxed. They're not regular pets — they've had special training for hospital visits. Pretty cool that dogs can have hospital jobs too, right? If you'd like to know when the next visit is, your care team can find out.

instruction: Why is there a person from a pharmacy here? I thought pharmacies are just stores.
response: Good question! A pharmacist doesn't just work at stores — hospitals have them too. The pharmacist at Children's Hospital helps make sure any medicine you're given is safe and the right amount for you. They also answer questions your parents might have about your medicine, like when to take it or if it might make your tummy feel funny. There's even a pharmacy right here on the first floor of the hospital near the B1 entrance. They're part of your care team, just like your doctor and nurse!

instruction: My doctor mentioned a social worker might come talk to my family. Are we in trouble?
response: Not at all — you're definitely not in trouble. Social workers at Children's Hospital are here to support families during what can be a really stressful time. They help with things like navigating the hospital system, connecting your family with community resources, sorting out financial concerns, and just providing someone to talk to when emotions are running high. Think of them as an advocate who's in your corner. Having a child in the hospital affects the whole family, and social workers help make sure everyone — not just the patient — has the support they need.

instruction: What's the difference between all the doctors I keep seeing? There's like three different ones.
response: It can feel like a revolving door, but each person has a specific role. Your attending physician is the senior doctor who oversees your entire care and makes the big decisions. Residents are doctors who've finished medical school and are doing specialized training — they work under your attending physician and are often the ones checking in more frequently. You might also see medical students, who are still in medical school and learning by participating in patient care under supervision. They all communicate with each other so everyone's on the same page about your treatment plan.

instruction: A nurse practitioner came in today. Is that different from a regular nurse?
response: Yeah, there's a real difference in scope. Registered nurses and registered practical nurses handle your day-to-day care — monitoring your condition, giving medications, coordinating appointments, and keeping your family informed. A nurse practitioner has additional advanced training and functions more like a doctor on the team. They partner with the medical staff, work closely with your attending physician to plan your care, and can do things like order tests or adjust treatment plans. Both roles are essential, but they operate at different levels of clinical decision-making.

instruction: Someone from something called the Gender Pathways Service left information for me. Who are they?
response: The Gender Pathways Service — often called GPS — is a multidisciplinary team at Children's Hospital that provides gender-affirming care for gender diverse and transgender young people up to age 17. They follow established North American and international guidelines, including those from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. If you're interested in learning more or connecting with them, you can reach out at gps@lhsc.on.ca or ask your care team to help you get in touch. It's completely your choice whether to engage with the service.

instruction: What does the physiotherapist actually do? One is supposed to come see me tomorrow.
response: A physiotherapist focuses on helping you with movement, strength, and physical recovery. Depending on your situation, they might work with you on exercises to rebuild strength, help you relearn how to move safely after a procedure, or assess things like how you'll manage getting around at home. They're also the ones who — along with occupational therapists — help figure out safe transportation options if you have mobility needs when it's time to go home. They're a standard part of the care team here, so their visit just means they want to check in on the physical side of your recovery.

instruction: I heard there's a psychologist available. Does that mean my care team thinks something's wrong with me mentally?
response: Not at all — it doesn't mean anyone thinks something is wrong with you. Paediatric psychologists at Children's Hospital work with kids and teens who are dealing with the challenges that come with being sick or hospitalized, which is stressful for literally anyone. They can help with coping strategies for managing physical and emotional symptoms, and they can also assess thinking and learning skills if a medical condition might be affecting those. It's a support resource, not a judgment. Wanting help processing a difficult experience is actually a pretty mature move.

instruction: What's the Transitions in Care team? My nurse mentioned them.
response: The Transitions in Care team is specifically focused on helping paediatric patients navigate big changes — like transitioning from youth care to adult care, or going from being in the hospital back to school. These transitions can be complicated and a bit overwhelming, so this team exists to make them smoother. If you're getting closer to aging out of paediatric services, or if you're trying to figure out how returning to school will work with your health needs, they're the people who can help coordinate that process. Ask your care team if you want more details about how they can support you.

instruction: Who's the person who came to talk to my mom about an ethics consultation?
response: That was likely someone from the clinical ethics consultation service. At LHSC, there are staff members who are specifically educated and trained to help when tough ethical decisions come up during patient care — situations where the right path forward isn't straightforward. They work with patients, families, and healthcare providers to identify and talk through those difficult questions. It doesn't mean something has gone wrong; it just means your care involves a complex decision, and having an ethics perspective can help everyone think it through more clearly.

instruction: Is there really a lawyer I can talk to at the hospital?
response: There actually is. Children's Hospital has a medical-legal partnership with Pro Bono Law Ontario, called PBLO. It's designed to help families identify and resolve legal issues that might be affecting a child's health or the family's ability to provide care. The service provides free legal assistance to low-income families whose child is either an inpatient or outpatient at Children's Hospital. You can't just walk in — a social worker would refer your case to the on-site triage lawyer. So if your family is dealing with a legal issue connected to your health situation, mention it to your care team and they can get the process started.

instruction: What's a spiritual care specialist? I'm not really religious.
response: Spiritual Care at LHSC is a professional service that's open to everyone, regardless of whether you follow a religion or not. Spiritual care practitioners work with patients and families on what matters most to them — that could be religious needs, but it could also be help with finding meaning during a hard time, processing grief, or just having someone listen without a medical agenda. There's also a sanctuary on the third floor of Zone C that's open around the clock for anyone who wants quiet time or a space to reflect. You can reach a Spiritual Care Specialist through your nurse at pager 14693 if you're ever curious.
